**Authors:** Andrew M. Camp, J. Cameron Anglum, Cory Koedel, Se Woong Lee, Tuan D. Nguyen  
**Review Date:** 2026-09-25  
**Model:** Claude (via Claude Code)  
**Review Mode:** Retrospective (Reader's Guide)

### Overall Assessment: Useful with Caveats

Camp, Anglum, Koedel, Lee, and Nguyen give the field the most current causal evidence on whether Missouri's four-day school week (4DSW) does what its adopters say it does: using statewide teacher-level administrative data from 2008–09 through 2023–24, a Gardner et al. two-stage difference-in-differences with not-yet-treated adopters as the only controls, and the full post-COVID wave that took Missouri from 33 to 178 four-day districts, they find that adoption did not detectably reduce teacher exits (−0.006, SE 0.007, on a pre-adoption base of 0.126; Table 2), did not raise the new-hire share of the workforce (0.001, SE 0.006; Table 3), and did shift the origin of new hires toward teachers from other Missouri districts (+0.011, SE 0.003) and away from teachers new to Missouri teaching (−0.010, SE 0.004). The retention null is the paper's load-bearing result and it holds up: flat pre-trends, stability across the saturation specification and the 151 spillover-exclusion thresholds, and a bias direction (poaching from not-yet-treated neighbors would make adoption look *good* for retention) that runs against a hidden benefit. It should replace or sit beside Thompson (2025) as the reference citation for Missouri, and it moves the multi-state literature — positive in Texas and modestly Arkansas, null in Colorado and Missouri/Oklahoma, negative in Oregon — further toward "little or no retention effect." The caveats attach to how the paper talks about that null and to its two secondary claims. "No evidence of practically meaningful 4DSW impacts" is a point-estimate sentence; the 95% interval reaches about 2 fewer exits per 100 teachers, roughly 16% of baseline turnover, which is not a tight zero and is larger than the composition shift the paper then interprets as "nontrivial." The abstract's "composition of new hires shifts toward more experienced teachers" restates an origin measure (from another Missouri district vs. new to Missouri teaching) as an experience measure the paper does not directly find (p. 21 reports insignificant experience effects, in an appendix not available to this review), and the paper's own Figure 5 shows the from-another-district estimate drifting toward zero and its band covering zero once controls within roughly the median mover distance (41 km) are excluded — a pattern the text reads permissively. The "perception versus reality" frame that the introduction calls the most interesting takeaway compares interviewees' claims about applicant volume and satisfaction, which the data never measure, with exit and hire-share outcomes, and it does not confront the fact that the one robust positive result is consistent with what superintendents describe. Add a cluster of production-level inconsistencies (an early/late adopter definition stated two ways; a Table 6 note describing district-level models as teacher-level; treatment timing indexed t+1 in Equations 1–2 and t in Equation 4; exit outcomes plotted under a "retention" axis label; 554 vs. 559 districts), no data availability, code, or software statement, and a supplement that carries every alternative-estimator, control-group, covariate, and pre-COVID robustness check, and the right posture is: rely on the retention null and quote its interval; cite the composition shift as a reallocation of experienced in-state movers with the spillover caveat attached; and treat the "information problem" framing as the authors' interpretation rather than a demonstrated finding.

#### Key Strengths

- The design is well chosen for the setting and executed with current tools. Adopters differ sharply from never-adopters (Table 1, Panel A: average salary \$44,718 vs. \$54,909; rural share 46.1% vs. 10.9%), so the paper compares adopters only with not-yet-treated adopters and uses the Gardner et al. (2024) two-stage estimator to block forbidden comparisons; it clusters at the district (about 178 clusters), omits covariates on principled grounds, and reports pre-adoption means so every estimate can be scaled.
- The retention null is the most robust object in the paper. It is stable across Table 2, the saturation model (−0.007, Table 5), the event study (Figure 2), and the spillover-exclusion path (Figure 4), it is not the product of an outcome definition a replicator could easily overturn, and the two plausible SUTVA violations (adopters recruit from neighbors; adoption follows a turnover spike) both bias *toward* finding a benefit, so a null survives them.
- The robustness program is unusually complete for the question: a Butts (2024) spatial-spillover test over every integer distance from 0 to 150 km, commuting-zone saturation interactions, a re-estimation using only the 22 interviewed districts as treated, a pre-COVID subsample, alternative control groups with covariate pre-trend plots, and three alternative staggered-DiD estimators — although all but the spillover and saturation exhibits live in a supplement this review could not open.
- The paper tests a practitioner belief against administrative data in the same state and sample. The 36 interviews (20 superintendents, 4 principals, 12 teachers in 22 districts) are thinly documented, but pairing them with the quantitative estimates, and then re-running the models on the interviewed districts alone, is a model for evaluating policies whose case rests on what adopters perceive.
- Prose and tables agree on every headline number. "0.6 fewer exits per 100," "1.3 fewer STEM exits," and "on the order of 1 FTE per 100" all match Tables 2 and 3; Table 2's exit components sum to any-turnover in every column; and the authors apply the von Hippel–Schuetze "no, but" caution to their own STEM coefficient.

#### Key Concerns

- The null is framed by its point estimate, not its interval. The introduction's "no evidence of practically meaningful 4DSW impacts" (p. 2) and the results' "very small" (p. 11) describe −0.006; the data are consistent with anything from a 2-point reduction (about 16% of baseline) to a small increase, and for STEM teachers with reductions of up to a quarter of baseline. The claim that vacancy confounding is "largely ruled out" by the retention null (p. 12) rests on the same point-estimate reasoning.
- The composition shift is less settled than the abstract implies. Figure 5 shows the from-another-district estimate moving toward zero as spillover-exposed controls are excluded, with the band including zero from roughly 50 km on — near the 41-km median move distance — and the paper's stated test (do the bands still cover the d = 0 estimate?) cannot distinguish "no bias" from "estimate no longer distinguishable from zero." The abstract's "more experienced teachers" is inferred from origin, not measured; the direct experience test is described as insignificant and underpowered (p. 21).
- The special-education "boost" featured in the introduction (p. 2) is one 10%-significant cell (0.022, SE 0.012) in a 12-estimate table, falls to 0.015 (SE 0.014) in the saturation specification (Table 6), and is exactly the kind of "no, but" subgroup result the authors warn against three pages earlier; only its from-another-district component (0.029, SE 0.006) is robust.
- The perception-vs-reality conclusion outruns the design. Interviewees' concrete evidence was applicant volume, which the paper cannot observe (note 10); the qualitative section gives no counts behind "overwhelmingly" or "a handful of dissenters"; and the paper's own significant result — more experienced in-state movers — is consistent with the recruitment advantage superintendents describe. Two cited predecessors (Thompson 2025; Camp 2024) report that nearby four-day adoption harms retention in five-day neighbors, which is not engaged; the spillover section tests bias in the treatment effect, not harm to non-adopters, and never reports the spillover coefficient itself.
- The reader must resolve several inconsistencies and take much on trust. Text (p. 6) and Table 1 note (p. 8) define the early/late split differently; Table 6's note calls district-level models "teacher-level"; Equations 1–2 index treatment at t+1 while Equation 4 uses t and the fixed-effect symbols change between them; Figures 2 and 4 plot exits under a "Change in Teacher Retention" axis; Table 1 sums to 554 districts against 559 in the text; Table 3, column 3's components sum to 0.115 against a reported 0.117; p. 21 speaks of excluding "nonrural, never-treated" districts when pp. 6 and 19 say the controls are not-yet-treated only. There is no data availability statement, access pathway, code, or software statement, the non-confidential adoption-year list is not released, and Appendices A–E carry the alternative estimators, covariates, control groups, interview-district test, pre-COVID sample, and salary/experience trends.

#### What to Rely On

- Adopting the four-day week in Missouri did not produce a detectable reduction in teacher turnover, overall or for high-need, STEM, or special-education teachers. Quote it as −0.006 (SE 0.007) on a pre-adoption mean of 0.126 (Table 2, Panel A row 1, col. 1) with flat pre-trends (Figure 2), and read it as "reductions larger than about 2 exits per 100 are unlikely," not as "the effect is zero."
- Adopting districts did not expand their teacher workforce, as measured by the new-hire share of FTE (0.001, SE 0.006; Table 3, Panel A row 1, col. 1), confirmed by the event study in Figure 3.
- The retention null does not depend on how saturated the local market already was at adoption: the 4DSW × prevalence interaction is 0.010 (SE 0.050) for any turnover (Table 5), and the main coefficients barely move when it is added. This extends Thompson (2025)'s Missouri null through the post-2019 wave.
- Adopters draw relatively more new hires from other Missouri districts and fewer who are new to Missouri teaching (Table 3, Panel A rows 2–3, col. 1: +0.011 and −0.010; about +23% and −13% of their pre-adoption means). Cite this as a reallocation of experienced in-state movers, with the Figure 5 caveat attached.
- The 4DSW did not detectably reduce out-of-field teaching in high-need fields (Table 4), though the estimates are imprecise and no baseline is reported.
- Educators in adopting districts overwhelmingly believe the policy helps recruitment and retention, and frame it as a substitute for salary (pp. 4–5). This is consistent with prior interview work in Arkansas and with the RAND multi-state study; cite it as confirmation, not discovery.
- Missouri's adopters are small, rural, lower-paying districts with higher baseline turnover (Table 1); the 178 districts contain 13% of the state's teachers and 12% of its students (Figure 1).

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- "No practically meaningful impact on retention" — the 95% interval runs to about −0.020, roughly 16% of baseline turnover and larger than the composition shift the paper interprets; the paper never states the range. For STEM teachers the interval admits reductions of about a quarter of baseline.
- "The composition of new hires shifts toward more experienced teachers" (abstract) — the measured variable is origin, not experience; the paper reports the direct experience test as insignificant (p. 21, appendix not available); and under the paper's own spillover exclusion the from-another-district estimate is not distinguishable from zero beyond about 50 km (Figure 5).
- "A boost in special education recruitment" (introduction) — one marginal cell in a 12-estimate table that loses significance in Table 6; only the from-another-district SPED component is robust.
- "No indication that spillover effects are causing bias" — the test asks whether the d = 0 estimate stays inside the bands, which it does even when the bands also include zero. For retention this is reassuring because the estimate is flat across d; for recruitment it is uninformative, and the paper does not report the spillover coefficient or test whether non-adopting neighbors are harmed, which two cited predecessors found.
- "Strong evidence of parallel pre-trends ... with small confidence intervals" — pre-period coefficients in two-stage/imputation event studies are computed from the same untreated observations used to fit the first stage, so their narrow bands (visibly narrower than post-period bands in Figures 2–3) are weaker evidence than they look; the event-study window, binning, and reference periods are unstated, and both −6 and −1 are pinned at zero.
- "The scope for saturation to influence the treatment effect is very small" — a point-estimate claim; scaled by the 0.095 SD, the interaction SE of 0.050 permits moderation of about ±1 point per SD, the same size as the effects at issue.
- "A substantial gap between perception and reality" / "a significant information problem" — the perceptions most concretely cited (applicant volume) are unmeasured, the interview sample is neither counted nor selected transparently, and the one robust positive result is consistent with what interviewees describe. Read as "perceived large gains are not visible in exit or hire-share data."
- The literature summary quoted from this paper — seven of the eight retention studies it cites are working papers; Thompson (2025) is characterized as "null in each state individually" (verify against its heterogeneity tables); the −0.02 to −0.09 SD achievement range excludes the cited Nowak et al. metropolitan estimate and omits Thompson's Oregon *Journal of Public Economics* study; Nowak et al. studied a suburban Denver-area district, not "Denver"; and the *EEPA* scoping review by Grant et al. is not cited.
- Any number a reader must reconstruct from the connective tissue: the early/late adopter cutoff (follow the text's "adopted by 2020–21 = early," which matches N = 106), the 554/559 district count, the Table 3 column 3 sum, the Table 4 observation counts (2,651–2,658 vs. 2,673), and the treatment-timing convention across Equations 1–4.
- Every "substantively similar" robustness claim — alternative estimators (A.3–A.5), covariates (A.2), district aggregation (A.1), alternative control groups and salary/experience trends (C), the interview-district test (D), and the pre-COVID sample (E) — is asserted in prose and lives in a supplement this review could not examine; none can be verified from the article, and none can be reproduced without DESE access, the authors' adoption-year file, and code the paper does not provide.

### Methods Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The paper uses a staggered-adoption difference-in-differences design. It estimates effects with the Gardner et al. (2024) two-stage imputation estimator on Missouri statewide administrative data and uses only not-yet-treated adopters as controls. This is a well-chosen, modern design, and it supports the paper's main retention claim: adoption did not produce a *large* drop in teacher turnover. Three other claims rest on weaker ground. The finding that districts did not expand their workforce is inferred indirectly. The one positive finding, a shift toward hires from other Missouri districts, visibly weakens in the paper's own spillover test (Figure 5). The special-education recruitment "boost" is significant only at the 10% level and does not survive the saturation specification. The wording "no practically meaningful" effect also claims more than the confidence interval can support.

**Strengths:**

- **The design fits the question, and the estimator suits staggered adoption.** Adoption is staggered from 2010–11 to 2024–25 (p. 7, Figure 1). The authors explain the "forbidden comparisons" problem in two-way fixed effects (p. 9) and use the two-stage estimator, which fits district and year fixed effects only on untreated observations (pp. 9–10, Eqs. 2–4). The paper says results are similar with Borusyak et al., Wooldridge, and Callaway–Sant'Anna estimators (p. 11). That claim lives in Supplemental Tables A.3–A.5, which were not available for this review.
- **The control group is chosen with good reason.** Table 1 Panel A shows that ever-adopters and never-adopters differ greatly. For example, average salary is \$44,718 versus \$54,909 and the rural share is 46.1% versus 10.9% (p. 8, Table 1, Panel A). The authors therefore compare adopters only with districts that have not adopted yet (p. 6), which moves identification to timing among eventual adopters. That is the right call for this setting.
- **The data are statewide and cover a long period.** They include every full-time teacher from 2008–09 to 2023–24 (p. 5) and so capture the post-COVID adoption wave, which grew the adopter count from 33 to 178 (p. 3). Checkable consistency: Table 2 is internally additive. Row 2 plus row 3 equals row 1 within rounding in every column, for both estimates and pre-adoption means; for example, 0.073 + 0.053 = 0.126 (p. 12, Table 2, Panel B, col. 1).
- **The retention null is reasonably precise and consistent across checks.** The main estimate is −0.006 (SE 0.007) against a pre-adoption mean of 0.126 (p. 12, Table 2, Panel A row 1 col. 1 and Panel B row 1 col. 1). The event study shows no posttreatment pattern (p. 13, Figure 2). The estimate barely moves when the saturation interaction is added: −0.007 (0.007) (p. 20, Table 5, Panel A, All subjects).
- **The robustness program is unusually broad.** It includes a Butts (2024) spatial-spillover test over 151 distance thresholds (pp. 14–16, Eq. 6; Figures 4–5, pp. 17–18), commuting-zone saturation interactions (p. 19, Eq. 7; Tables 5–6, p. 20), and a test of whether the interviewed districts did unusually well (p. 21). It also includes a pre-COVID-only sample (pp. 21–22), alternative control groups, and covariate pre-trend checks (pp. 19–21). The last four of these are reported only in appendices that were not available for review.
- **The authors are candid about limits.** They acknowledge that the recruitment outcome depends on vacancies (pp. 10–11). They warn against "no, but" subgroup inference for the STEM retention coefficient (p. 11) and note that exits from the profession cannot be separated from cross-state moves (p. 24, note 11).

**Weaknesses:**

- **"No practically meaningful effect" goes beyond what the retention confidence interval shows.** The −0.006 (0.007) estimate (p. 12, Table 2) gives a 95% CI of about [−0.020, +0.008] (my calculation). Relative to the 0.126 pre-adoption mean (same table, Panel B), the data cannot rule out a turnover reduction of about 2 points, or roughly 16% of baseline. That is not trivial for a zero-cost amenity. The paper describes the effect using the point estimate: "just 0.6 fewer teacher exits per 100 teacher FTEs" (p. 11). For STEM teachers, −0.013 (0.008) against a mean of 0.109 (p. 12, Table 2, col. 3) leaves reductions of up to about a quarter of baseline inside the CI (my calculation). (Interpretive.)
- **The composition-shift finding weakens in the paper's own spillover test.** The main estimates are +0.011** (0.003) for hires from another Missouri district and −0.010* (0.004) for hires new to teaching in Missouri (p. 14, Table 3, Panel A rows 2–3, col. 1). The text says these estimates "converge toward zero at high values of d, but the error bands include the original estimates at virtually all values of d" (p. 16). Reading Figure 5 (p. 18) visually, the "Moves to District" band includes zero from about 50 km onward, and the point estimate is near zero beyond about 100 km. The "New to Teaching" band includes zero at most thresholds beyond about 15–20 km. Median distance for cross-district moves is 41 km (p. 24, note 13), so this is exactly the range where spillovers are plausible. Overlapping bands are not a test that two estimates are equal. Under Butts's logic, estimates that move toward zero as spillover-exposed controls are removed are what one would expect if part of the main estimate reflects contaminated controls. Lost precision and a changing control sample are other explanations. (Figure reading is approximate; the interpretation is mine.)
- **The special-education "boost" is fragile, yet it is featured in the introduction.** The introduction reports "a boost in special education recruitment" (p. 2). Its basis is 0.022+ (0.012), significant only at the 10% level (p. 14, Table 3, Panel A row 1 col. 4), in a table with 12 estimates and no multiplicity adjustment. In the saturation specification the total SPED new-hire estimate falls to 0.015 (0.014) and is not significant (p. 20, Table 6, Panel A, In SPED). The component "from another district" estimate is robust: 0.029** (0.006) on p. 14 and 0.025** (0.007) in Table 6, Panel B, p. 20. The "no, but" caution the authors apply to STEM retention (p. 11) applies equally here.
- **The flat pre-trends in the event studies are weaker evidence than the text says.** The text says the event studies "show strong evidence of parallel pre-trends ... with small confidence intervals and point estimates near zero" (p. 11). In Figure 2 (p. 13) and Figure 3 (p. 15), the pre-period bands are visibly much narrower than the post-period bands. With imputation and two-stage estimators, pre-period coefficients come from the same untreated observations used to fit the first-stage fixed effects. They are therefore partly pulled toward zero and cannot be compared directly with post-period coefficients (see Roth's 2024 discussion of event studies from recent DiD estimators). The paper does not say how the leads were constructed. It also does not say whether the endpoints (−6, +6) are binned, although event time −1 is plotted as a zero reference with no band. (Interpretive; the figure description is checkable.)
- **"Recruitment" is measured by hiring volume, not recruitment success.** The outcome is the new-hire FTE share (p. 10, Eq. 5). It cannot capture applicant pools, the quality of hires, or unfilled vacancies. The authors say application data are unavailable (p. 23–24, note 10), and those are the outcomes interviewees actually cited (p. 5). The conclusion that there is "no workforce expansion" (p. 12) is inferred from a null new-hire share combined with a null retention estimate. The paper does not estimate total FTE or pupil–teacher ratios directly in the main text.
- **"More experienced teachers" is a loose label.** The abstract says new hires shift "toward more experienced teachers" (p. 1). The underlying measure is origin: hires from another Missouri district versus hires "new to teaching in Missouri" (p. 14, Table 3). The claim that the second group are "most[ly] ... novices" (p. 2) has no supporting number in the main text. The paper also reports no significant effect on average teacher experience (p. 21, citing Appendix Figure C.4, which was not available).
- **The late-period control group is thin and selected.** Identification uses only the 178 eventual adopters. My arithmetic supports this: 2,673 district-years (p. 14, Table 3) divided by 178 districts (p. 8, Table 1) is about 15 years per district. By visual reading of Figure 1 (p. 7), the adopter share goes from roughly 31% in 2023–24 to 32% (178 districts) in 2024–25. So the not-yet-treated controls in the final panel years are a small group of the latest adopters. Year effects for the post-COVID period, when most adoption happened, therefore rest on few districts. The paper does not report how many controls remain in each year. At long event horizons such as +6 (p. 13, Figure 2), coefficients come only from early cohorts.
- **Saturation tests are low-powered and measured only once.** Prevalence is measured once, at adoption (p. 19). That makes it largely collinear with adoption cohort and region. By my calculation, the interaction SE of 0.050 (p. 20, Table 5, Panel A) times the reported SD of about 0.095 (Table 5 note, p. 20) gives about 0.005 per SD of prevalence. So moderation of about ±1 point per SD cannot be ruled out. That is the same size as the effects at issue.
- **Minor checkable reporting inconsistencies:**
  - The text defines early adopters as those that "adopted the 4DSW by 2020–2021" (p. 6). The Table 1 note says "Late adopters are defined as adopters in 2020–2021 or later" (p. 8). Early-adopter N = 106 (p. 8) is consistent with the text's definition, given roughly 19% of 559 districts treated by 2020–21 in Figure 1 (p. 7; visual reading).
  - The Table 6 note says "Teacher-level regressions" (p. 20), but the table reports 2,673 district-years, and the parallel Table 3 note says "District level regressions weighted by teacher FTE" (p. 14).
  - In Table 3, Panel B, col. 3 (p. 14), 0.048 + 0.067 = 0.115, not the reported 0.117. The gap exceeds rounding. Other columns add up.
  - In Table 1, Panel A, 376 + 178 = 554 districts (p. 8), while the text reports 559 districts (p. 6).
  - The y-axes in Figures 2 and 4 (pp. 13, 17) are labeled "Change in Teacher Retention," but the plotted outcome is turnover, so negative values mean better retention.
- **The qualitative evidence is thinly documented.** It comes from 36 interviewees in 22 districts (p. 4), all in adopting districts, with deductive coding. The paper gives no protocol, no coding-reliability information, and no count of how many respondents held each view. Interviewing only current staff of adopting districts excludes teachers who left. This matters because the paper's "most interesting takeaway" is the gap between the interviews and the quantitative results (p. 2).

**Guidance for Readers:**

- **Rely on:** Adopting the four-day week (4DSW) in Missouri did not produce a *large* reduction in teacher turnover, for all teachers or for STEM and SPED teachers (p. 12, Table 2). Read this as "effects above about 2 percentage points (≈16% of baseline) are unlikely." Do not read it as "the effect is zero" or "small effects are ruled out." When comparing with the positive Arkansas and Texas estimates cited on p. 3, check whether those point estimates fall inside this paper's CI.
- **Treat with caution:** The finding that adopters draw more hires from other Missouri districts (p. 14, Table 3, row 2). It is statistically strong in the main specification but visibly weaker once controls within about the median mover distance are excluded (p. 18, Figure 5). Even if real, it is partly a reallocation among Missouri districts rather than a net gain in teacher supply.
- **Do not build on:** The special-education total-recruitment "boost" (0.022+, p. 14) by itself. The SPED from-another-district estimate is the more robust part.
- **"No workforce expansion"** means "no detectable change in the new-hire share of FTE." It says nothing about applicant volume, the quality of hires, or vacancy-fill rates. Those were the gains interviewees reported, and this paper cannot test them.
- **Scope:** The estimates are teacher-weighted average effects on the treated for Missouri adopters, pooled over observed durations. Most post-adoption years come from the post-2019 wave, which has short follow-up. They do not tell you what a never-adopting suburban district would get from adopting. Large adopters carry weight: one suburban district is about 21% of late-adopter teacher weight (p. 23, note 7).
- **Before citing robustness to alternative estimators, covariates, control groups, the interviewed-district subsample, or the pre-COVID sample**, check Supplemental Appendices A–E. This review could not verify them.
- **The qualitative–quantitative "disconnect" (p. 2)** is best read as "perceived large gains are not visible in turnover or hiring-volume data." It is not a direct refutation, because the interviews and the regressions partly concern different outcomes.

**Detailed Commentary:**

**Design and identification.** The question is how adopting a four-day week affects teacher retention and hiring. Staggered adoption across 178 of 559 Missouri districts (p. 6) is a natural setting for event-study DiD. Two choices strengthen credibility. First, restricting controls to not-yet-treated adopters directly addresses the very large level differences between adopters and non-adopters in Table 1, Panel A (p. 8). Second, the two-stage estimator avoids using already-treated districts as controls, which matters because adoption-timing heterogeneity is plausible here (p. 9). One caveat on Table 1, Panel B: it uses 2023–24 data (p. 8), when nearly all districts in both groups are treated. It is therefore not a pre-treatment balance comparison, and the significant early–late gap in turnover (−3.3 points, p. 8, Table 1, Panel B) partly reflects treatment duration. The substantive identification risk is that adoption timing responds to district-specific staffing shocks. Adoption after a turnover spike would produce mean reversion that looks like a *retention benefit*. The null result is therefore somewhat protected against that direction of bias. A shock that persists, such as a deteriorating local labor market, would bias toward zero. The flat pre-period coefficients argue against both. However, the pre-period coefficients in imputation-style event studies are mechanically well-behaved, as the Weaknesses section explains, so this reassurance is weaker than "strong evidence of parallel pre-trends" (p. 11) implies. The covariate event studies across three control-group definitions (pp. 19–21) help, but they are in Appendix C, which was not available.

**Timing and outcome construction.** The retention outcome is an exit after year t, and the treatment is 4DSW status in t+1 (p. 6, Eq. 1). This correctly assigns end-of-year exit decisions to the calendar teachers expect next year. Recruitment is the new-hire share in year t under year-t status (p. 10, Eq. 5). Both choices are sensible. The "left Missouri educator workforce" category combines cross-state moves, moves to private schools, and exits from teaching (p. 6; p. 24, note 11). This is standard with state data, but it means the decomposition in row 3 is coarse. Restricting to teachers at FTE ≥ 0.75 (p. 6) excludes part-time staff, and note 5 (p. 23) says results are similar without this restriction.

**Estimation and inference.** Standard errors are clustered by district (p. 9), which gives about 178 clusters (the ever-adopter count, p. 8, Table 1). That is adequate for cluster-robust inference. District clustering does not address spatially correlated shocks across neighboring districts. Given the paper's own evidence that teacher labor markets are local (p. 16), commuting-zone clustering would have been a useful check; its absence probably matters little for a null result. District-level recruitment regressions are FTE-weighted (p. 10). This keeps them comparable with the teacher-level retention models, but it also means larger districts dominate. The paper lists no covariates in the main specification and gives a principled reason (p. 9). Estimates with covariates are in Appendix Table A.2, which was not available. The text reports that the STEM retention coefficient becomes significant at the 10% level there (p. 11).

**Spillovers and saturation.** Using Butts's (2024) method is a real contribution, and the retention panels of Figure 4 (p. 17) are mostly stable across distance thresholds. One exception: a narrow window around 43–50 km shows an any-turnover estimate near −0.04, and by visual reading its band appears to exclude zero (p. 17, Figure 4, top panel). With 151 correlated estimates this is most likely noise, but the figure is not uniformly flat. The more consequential pattern is in Figure 5 (p. 18). The composition estimates move toward zero and lose significance as controls near adopters are excluded. That pattern is in the paper, but the text reads it permissively. An additional SUTVA concern cuts in a known direction for retention. If adopters recruit teachers away from neighboring not-yet-treated districts, turnover in the controls rises, which would bias the retention estimate toward showing a *benefit*. The retention null therefore holds up against this concern. For saturation (p. 19, Eq. 7), prevalence is measured only at adoption, varies mostly across cohorts and regions, and yields interaction estimates that are imprecise relative to the effects at stake (Weaknesses). "No evidence of moderation" is a fair summary. "Scope for saturation … is very small" (p. 19) is stronger than the SEs support.

**What is load-bearing.** The retention null rests on the most robust evidence. It is stable across Table 2, Table 5, Figure 2, and Figure 4, and it survives the plausible directions of bias. The recruitment null (p. 14, Table 3, row 1, col. 1: 0.001, SE 0.006) is also stable, but it answers a narrow question about hiring volume. The composition shift is the paper's only statistically strong positive result. It is plausible but depends on specification, specifically on whether spillover-exposed controls are included. Given the direction of the Figure 5 pattern, readers should not treat its magnitude (about 1 FTE per 100, p. 12) as a settled causal effect. The SPED results are mixed. The inflow from other districts is robust, but the total recruitment effect is not. Overall, the design is appropriate and competently executed, and the retention conclusion is credible. The paper's framing, though, sometimes claims more precision (retention), more robustness (composition), or broader meaning ("recruitment", "more experienced") than the estimates support. Several robustness claims depend on appendices this review could not examine, which limits confidence.

---

### Literature Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The paper places itself well within the narrow, fast-moving literature on the four-day school week (4DSW) and teacher labor markets. It cites nearly every close antecedent through 2025 and describes most of them accurately. Its account has three gaps readers should know about. First, it does not engage with prior evidence that nearby 4DSW adoption harms retention in *non-adopting* districts, including the first author's own earlier work. Second, it undersells how much of its recruitment finding was already seen in Missouri by Thompson (2025). Third, it leaves out the adjacent literatures in economics, organizational psychology, and evidence use that would explain its most-emphasized result: educators' optimism is not matched by the quantitative data.

**Strengths:**

- **Current coverage of the closest studies.** The Background section cites the 4DSW teacher-retention studies by state: Arkansas (Camp, 2024), Texas (Khalid, 2025; Lawson, 2025), Oregon (Ainsworth et al., 2024), Colorado (Morton & Dewil, 2024; Bowser, 2025), and Missouri/Oklahoma (Thompson, 2025). It adds the single-district Colorado study (Nowak et al., 2023) in endnote 2 (p. 3; endnote on p. 23). I checked each abstract on the web. The directional summaries hold up: Texas shows larger positive effects (Khalid reports about 3 percentage points; Lawson reports 2.7 percentage points), Oregon shows higher turnover, and Colorado shows null or small negative effects.
- **Candid about conflicting results.** The Conclusion states that positive effects are concentrated in one state, Texas (p. 22). It does not present the null as the only finding in the literature. The paper also takes up Oregon's opposite-signed result and gives a possible mechanism: slower salary growth in adopting districts, tested against Missouri data (p. 21). I checked Ainsworth et al.'s working paper on the web, and that salary finding appears there.
- **Directly addresses its nearest predecessor.** The paper names Thompson (2025) as "most directly related" (p. 3). It gives specific reasons its work differs: a longer panel through 2023–2024, the post-COVID wave that took Missouri from 33 to 178 4DSW districts (p. 3), recruitment outcomes, and interviews. It also runs a pre-COVID subsample to compare with Thompson over the same years (pp. 21–22).
- **Up-to-date methods citations.** The staggered-adoption DiD literature is cited correctly (Callaway & Sant'Anna; Goodman-Bacon; Sun & Abraham; Borusyak et al.; Gardner et al.; Roth et al.; pp. 6, 9–10). It uses Butts (2024) for spatial spillovers (p. 14) and von Hippel & Schuetze (2025) to warn against over-reading subgroup results when the main effect is null (p. 11).
- **Places the qualitative evidence alongside the Arkansas interview work.** The Missouri superintendent interviews are compared with superintendent interviews in Arkansas (Barnes & McKenzie, 2023; p. 4) and with Turner et al. (2019) (p. 2).

**Weaknesses:**

- **Earlier findings of spillovers onto non-adopting districts are not discussed.** The spillover section treats spillovers only as a possible source of bias. It concludes there is "no indication that spillover effects are causing bias" (pp. 14–18; Figures 4–5). The paper never mentions that two studies it cites found harmful spillovers on nearby five-day districts:
  - *Checkable, web-verified:* Thompson's (2025) EER abstract reports that higher 4DSW prevalence in the local labor market "leads to increased teacher turnover." It says this is driven partly by 4DSW districts recruiting teachers out of nearby five-day districts.
  - *Web, from a search-result summary:* Camp's (2024) working paper reports "suggestive evidence" of harm to retention in nearby non-adopting schools.
  
  The paper's endnote 15 (p. 24) mentions Thompson's local-saturation result only briefly and says it is "driven primarily by teachers exiting the profession." The abstract (web-verified) credits it partly to poaching from nearby five-day districts, with profession exits rising as saturation grows. Readers should not treat this paper's spillover test as having overturned those findings. The test was built to check whether the treatment effect is biased, and the text does not report the spillover coefficient itself.
- **The composition finding is presented as more novel than it is.** The paper treats recruitment and new-hire composition as an extension beyond Thompson (p. 3). It compares its composition shift only to Lawson's Texas results (p. 12). Thompson's abstract (web-verified) already reports that Missouri/Oklahoma 4DSW districts recruit teachers from nearby five-day districts. That is essentially the same mechanism as this paper's finding of more hires from other Missouri districts and fewer new to Missouri (Table 3, p. 14: +0.011 and −0.010). Morton & Dewil (2024) also studied a recruitment outcome, the share of teachers holding shortage credentials. That outcome is close to this paper's out-of-field "stress indicators" (Table 4, p. 16), but the paper does not draw the parallel.
- **The description of Thompson (2025) may be over-simplified.** The paper says Thompson "finds null retention effects overall in a pooled analysis and in each state individually" (p. 3). Thompson's abstract (web-verified) says beneficial effects are "most prevalent … in states where the four-day school week is motivated by teacher recruitment and retention efforts" and among several teacher subgroups. From the abstract alone I cannot tell which state this refers to or whether the state-specific estimates are significant. Check Thompson's state-by-state tables before repeating "null in each state." This matters because the two papers cover overlapping Missouri data.
- **The comparison to Lawson leaves out a key contrast.** The paper calls its recruitment findings "substantively similar" to Lawson's Texas results (p. 12). Lawson's abstract (web, via a fetch summary) reports that incoming cohorts' experience and education did *not* change, even though more hires came from other districts. This paper's abstract says new hires shift "toward more experienced teachers" (p. 1). That claim rests on where hires came from, not on measured experience. The paper's own district-level experience results are small and not significant (p. 21; the supporting appendix figures were not available for this review).
- **Omission: a 4DSW scoping review in the same journal.** Grant et al. (2025/2026) published a scoping review of empirical 4DSW research in *EEPA* (web-verified). It identified 123 studies as of November 2024, about three-quarters of them gray literature. This paper was revised in January and April 2026 (p. 1) and does not cite it. The review is the obvious companion reading for gauging how thin and gray this literature is.
- **The retention evidence base is mostly unpublished, and the paper does not say so.** *Checkable:* seven of the eight 4DSW teacher-retention studies cited (pp. 3, 22, endnote 2) are working papers in the reference list (pp. 24–26): Ainsworth et al.; Bowser; Camp; Khalid; Lawson; Morton & Dewil; Nowak et al. Only Thompson (2025) is a journal article. The paper also calls the literature both "growing" (p. 3) and "thin" (p. 22) without noting that it rests mostly on unrefereed work, including a working paper by the first author.
- **The student-outcomes summary is incomplete and firms up between sections.**
  - The −0.02 to −0.09 SD effect-size range (p. 4) excludes Nowak et al. (2023). The paper cites Nowak for "negative impacts on student academic outcomes" (endnote 2, p. 23), and Nowak's abstract (web-verified) reports declines of 0.2–0.3 SD.
  - Thompson's widely cited Oregon achievement study (*Journal of Public Economics*, 2021; web-verified) is missing from the reference list.
  - Morton & Dewil (2024) is grouped with studies finding "small and statistically insignificant impacts on average daily attendance" (p. 4). Its CALDER summary (web-verified) reports a 0.76-percentage-point attendance decline in non-rural schools.
  - The description moves from "most studies find the 4DSW reduces student achievement, though … only … about half the time" (p. 4) to "most prior research shows the 4DSW harms students' academic outcomes" (p. 22).
- **Little engagement with adjacent disciplines.** The paper's headline interpretation is a gap between perception and reality (pp. 2, 22). It is explained through reasoning about counterfactuals and "confirmation bias," with no citations. Several relevant literatures are missing:
  - economics work on how workers value schedule amenities and on compensating differentials;
  - the teacher working-conditions and turnover literature;
  - organizational-psychology research on compressed workweeks, which has long found that satisfaction rises without matching behavioral change;
  - research on how education leaders form beliefs and use evidence.
  
  The paper also does not tie its "keeping up with the Joneses" framing (p. 4) to the policy-diffusion study co-written by one of its own authors, Anglum & Park (2021). That study is cited only for adoption rationale (p. 3).

**Guidance for Readers:**

- **Cite this paper** for: extending Missouri 4DSW retention evidence through the post-COVID adoption wave (p. 3); a null estimate that is precisely estimated relative to the pre-adoption mean (−0.006 against a mean of 0.126; Table 2, p. 12); the side-by-side of interviews and administrative data (pp. 4–5, 22); and the saturation analysis that includes the post-2019 wave (p. 19).
- **Cite Thompson (2025) instead, or as well,** for: the first Missouri 4DSW retention evidence; the finding that 4DSW districts recruit teachers from nearby five-day districts; and area-level effects of local 4DSW prevalence on turnover and exit. Read Thompson's own heterogeneity results before repeating this paper's claim of "null … in each state individually" (p. 3).
- **Cite Camp (2024) and Thompson (2025) together** for the possibility that the 4DSW redistributes teachers among nearby districts rather than increasing supply. Do not read this paper's spillover section (pp. 14–18) as ruling that out. That section tests whether the treatment effect is biased, not whether non-adopters are harmed.
- **Companion reading on the 4DSW evidence base:** Grant et al., "The Four-Day School Week at K–12 Schools in the United States: A Scoping Review of Empirical Research Evidence," *EEPA* (online 2025; web-verified). Also useful: Morton & Klinenberg, CALDER Brief 43 (Feb. 2026; web-verified). That brief shows, with Texas data, that districts labeled "4DSW" differ widely in their actual calendars. This bears on comparing Missouri with the positive Texas studies and on treating the 4DSW as a single yes/no policy. Thompson & Ward (2022) is cited only for student achievement (endnote 4, p. 23), but the same variation in how the policy is carried out could matter for teachers.
- **Companion reading on student outcomes:** Thompson (2021), "Is four less than five?", *Journal of Public Economics* (Oregon achievement; web-verified; not in this paper's references). Add Nowak et al. (2023) for a metropolitan district, where estimated achievement losses (0.2–0.3 SD per its abstract) are much larger than the range the paper reports (p. 4).
- **Verify before repeating:**
  - (a) "approximately 850" 4DSW districts in 2023, attributed to Morton et al. (2024) (p. 1). Morton & Dewil's CALDER summary (web) says "roughly 900 … as of 2023," so counts vary by source.
  - (b) The cost-savings statement attributing a 24-state, 1–2% finding to Thompson et al. (2021) (p. 3). That paper's abstract (web) describes a national study of adoption and implementation and says adoption is "often financially motivated." The paper cites the same study for teacher recruitment and retention being "the more prevalent rationale" contemporarily (p. 3). A working-paper version of Thompson (2021, *National Tax Journal*), the expenditure study, reports 3.1% lower operating spending per pupil (web, IZA abstract). I could not access the full texts to settle which source supports which number.
  - (c) The Conclusion's "Nowak et al. (2023) find negative retention effects in … Denver" (p. 22). The study is of 27J Schools (Brighton), a suburban district in the Denver metro area (web-verified), as endnote 2 correctly says (p. 23). It is not Denver Public Schools.
- **Adjacent literatures that sharpen the interpretation** (from memory, verify):
  - Mas & Pallais (2017, *AER*) and Maestas et al. (2023, *JPE*) on how much workers value schedule flexibility and working conditions.
  - Baltes et al. (1999, *Journal of Applied Psychology*), a meta-analysis on compressed workweeks, which reports satisfaction gains without matching changes in absenteeism. This parallels the paper's finding that teachers like the policy but do not change their behavior.
  - Nguyen, Pham, Crouch & Springer (2020, *Educational Research Review*), a meta-analysis of teacher attrition and retention (a co-author of this paper is an author there).
  - Post-pandemic teacher labor-market studies, relevant to the paper's counterfactual argument (p. 22) that conditions may also have changed in non-adopting districts.
  - Research on how education policymakers use evidence, relevant to the "information problem" framing (p. 2).

**Detailed Commentary:**

**Where the paper sits.** This is one of about ten quasi-experimental studies of how the 4DSW affects teachers. Nearly all appeared as working papers between 2023 and 2025. The paper's reading of that literature is mostly accurate:

- **Positive:** Texas, with two studies of about 3 percentage points (Khalid; Lawson), and Arkansas, small (Camp).
- **Null or small negative:** Colorado (Morton & Dewil; Bowser) and Missouri/Oklahoma pooled (Thompson).
- **Negative:** Oregon (Ainsworth et al.) and one Colorado suburban district (Nowak et al.).

The paper's Missouri null (Table 2, p. 12) sits comfortably inside that spread. It adds one more state to the null side. It is also the only estimate so far that spans Missouri's post-2020 adoption surge (33 to 178 districts; p. 3). A reader who only reads the Background and Conclusion (pp. 3, 22) gets a fair map of *signs by state*. What the reader does not get is how immature the evidence is. The one peer-reviewed antecedent is Thompson (2025) (reference list, pp. 24–26). The *EEPA* scoping review by Grant et al., which reports that about 75% of 123 4DSW studies are gray literature (web-verified), is not cited. That omission stands out given that it appeared in the same journal while this paper was under revision.

**The main missing engagement is spillovers.** The paper's most technically careful section estimates the treatment effect after dropping "spillover-contaminated" control districts at distances from 0 to 150 km (p. 16), following Butts (2024). It concludes there is no bias. The research question, though, is whether the 4DSW helps adopting districts compete for teachers. The natural worry is that any gain comes at nearby districts' expense. Both Thompson (2025) and Camp (2024) report findings along those lines (web). Thompson's abstract says rising local 4DSW prevalence increases turnover, partly through 4DSW districts recruiting from nearby five-day districts. Camp (2024) reports suggestive harm to retention in nearby non-adopting schools.

This paper's composition result points the same way: more hires from other Missouri districts, fewer new to Missouri (Table 3, p. 14). The paper does not connect these pieces. Its endnote on Thompson's area-level result (endnote 15, p. 24) is brief and, compared with Thompson's abstract, incomplete. For readers, the policy implication differs a lot. "The 4DSW does nothing" and "the 4DSW moves experienced teachers between nearby districts without adding to supply" are different conclusions. The combined evidence fits the second at least as well as the first.

**Novelty claims.** The paper's stated contributions relative to Thompson (p. 3) are the newer data, recruitment and new-hire composition, and the qualitative component. The newer data is a real contribution. The recruitment contribution is partly anticipated: Thompson's abstract already describes the poaching mechanism in the same state. Lawson (2025) documents a larger version of the same shift toward within-state hires in Texas, and the paper acknowledges this (p. 12). The qualitative contribution is the most distinctive and the one the paper emphasizes most ("perhaps the most interesting takeaway," p. 2). Still, the finding that leaders perceive recruitment advantages is well established. The RAND study the paper cites (Kilburn et al., 2021) reported, per a 2026 *EdWeek* summary (web), that district leaders in its study states believed the 4DSW gave them recruitment and retention advantages. Barnes & McKenzie (2023) found the same in Arkansas. What is new here is the pairing of interviews and administrative data *in the same state and sample*. That includes the test using only the 22 interviewed districts as the treated group (p. 21; the appendix was not available for review). Readers should cite the paper for that pairing, not for the discovery that educators are enthusiastic.

**Accuracy spot-checks.** Most characterizations I could check against abstracts hold up:

- the direction and rough size of the Texas, Oregon, and Colorado results (p. 3);
- Oregon's salary-lag finding (p. 21);
- Ainsworth et al.'s teacher-FTE increase (p. 11). Ainsworth et al. suggest it may reflect adopters using savings to *avoid layoffs* during the recession rather than filling unmet hiring needs, so it is weaker support than the paper implies for the idea that more hiring signals success.

Items worth checking before repeating are listed under Guidance: Thompson's state-level heterogeneity, Morton & Dewil's attendance result, the Nowak location, the attribution of the cost-savings figures, and the effect-size range. None of these changes the paper's own estimates. Several of them change what "the literature shows" when that phrase is quoted from this paper. One example: the achievement range of −0.02 to −0.09 SD (p. 4) comes from a selected set of studies. It leaves out the paper's own cited metropolitan case and the most-cited Oregon study.

**Adjacent fields.** The paper is written in the economics-of-education tradition, and its methods citations are excellent. Its interpretive framing does not draw on other traditions.

- **Economics:** The 4DSW is a non-wage amenity in a market where districts compete. Compensating-differentials theory and the literature valuing schedule flexibility predict that a widely shared amenity will stop making any one district stand out. The superintendents quoted on p. 5 say exactly this, and the saturation analysis (pp. 19–21) is built to test it. The paper's own literature review never states that theory.
- **Organizational psychology:** Research on compressed workweeks (from memory, verify) has long found higher satisfaction without matching changes in behavior such as absenteeism. That is close to the paper's reconciliation that teachers value the policy "but not enough" to change jobs (p. 22).
- **Evidence use in education leadership:** The "information problem" framing (p. 2) and the confirmation-bias explanation (p. 22) are offered without citations. There is a body of work on how education leaders form causal beliefs and use research.
- **Post-pandemic teacher labor market:** Turnover rose in many places after 2021. That context bears directly on the paper's counterfactual argument (p. 22) and on how to read estimates that are heavily weighted toward post-2021 adopters.

None of these omissions undermines the estimates. They do mean readers get a thinner explanation of *why* a popular policy fails to move behavior than the paper's framing promises.

**Limits of this assessment.** I checked the cited working papers' abstracts on the web. I did not read their full texts, and several publisher pages were paywalled. The online Supplemental Appendices were not available, so I make no claims about their contents. Items marked "from memory, verify" should be checked before they are relied on.

*Web sources consulted (September 2026):* Thompson (2025) abstract, ideas.repec.org/a/eee/ecoedu/v109y2025ics0272775725000883.html; Morton & Dewil (2024), caldercenter.org/publications/impacts-four-day-school-weeks-teacher-recruitment-and-retention-and-student-attendance; Ainsworth et al. (2024), edworkingpapers.com/ai24-1035 (full PDF); Lawson (2025), edworkingpapers.com/ai25-1372; Khalid (2025), edre.uark.edu/_resources/pdf/edrewp2025-09.pdf; Bowser (2025), edworkingpapers.com/ai25-1208; Nowak et al. (2023), edworkingpapers.com/ai23-721; Camp (2024), edworkingpapers.com/ai24-971 (search summary); Grant et al. scoping review, journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.3102/01623737251362865 and hedcoinstitute.uoregon.edu; Morton & Klinenberg, CALDER Brief 43-0226; Thompson (2021, JPubE), ideas.repec.org/a/eee/pubeco/v193y2021ics0047272720301729.html; Thompson (2021, NTJ) IZA DP 12698; Thompson et al. (2021, EFP) abstract via direct.mit.edu; NCTQ (Nov. 2025) and EdWeek (Apr. 2026) summaries.
