### Writing Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The paper is compact, well sequenced, and its core results (Table 2 row 1, Table 3 rows 2–3) are reported in the text accurately; every headline number I checked against the rendered tables matches. The weaknesses are in how the evidence is framed. The introduction, abstract, and conclusion describe a null that the tables show is imprecise, and they call a qualitative–quantitative "disconnect" more definitive than the evidence allows. The paper also has a cluster of production-level inconsistencies (the early/late adopter definition, a table note describing the wrong unit of analysis, equation notation, figure axis labels, district counts) that a careful reader has to resolve on their own.

**Strengths:**

- **Clear architecture.** The sequence runs Background, then Qualitative motivation (pp. 4–5), Data, Methods, Results, Extensions, Other Considerations, and Conclusion. Each results paragraph tells the reader which panel, row, and column it discusses (e.g., p. 11, "panel A row (1) and column (1)"), so the argument is easy to track against Tables 2–3.
- **Numbers in the prose match the tables.** Examples: "0.6 fewer teacher exits per 100" (p. 11) matches −0.006 (p. 12, Table 2, Panel A row 1 col 1). "1.3 fewer STEM teacher exits per 100" (p. 11) matches −0.013 (Table 2, Panel A row 1 col 3). A "shift … on the order of 1 teacher FTE per 100" (p. 12) matches 0.011** / −0.010* (p. 14, Table 3, Panel A rows 2–3 col 1).
- **Pre-adoption means are reported** (Table 2 and Table 3, Panel B), so readers can scale the point estimates. The decompositions add up: exits by type sum to any-turnover in every column of Table 2 (e.g., 0.073 + 0.053 = 0.126, p. 12, Table 2 Panel B col 1), and new-hire origins sum to all new hires in Table 3 col 1 (0.048 + 0.079 = 0.127, p. 14).
- **Candid about weak subgroup findings.** The text warns against over-reading the STEM coefficient and cites von Hippel & Schuetze on "no, but" heterogeneity (p. 11). It labels the SPED new-hire result "marginally significant" (p. 12), which matches the + marker on 0.022 (p. 14, Table 3, Panel A row 1 col 4).
- **Useful table notes on scaling.** The saturation table notes (p. 20, Tables 5–6) explain that the interaction coefficient is an "(infeasible)" 0-to-100% effect and give the SD of the moderator (≈0.095). Without that, the raw interaction coefficients would be easy to misread.
- **Figures 4–5 map d = 0 back to the main tables**, and their upper axes mark percentiles of the mover-distance distribution. The P50 tick sits near 41 km, which is consistent with footnote 13's "half occur within 41 km" (p. 24; Figs. 4–5, pp. 17–18).

**Weaknesses:**

- **The framing of the null outruns its precision (interpretive).** The introduction says the analysis "yields no evidence of practically meaningful 4DSW impacts" (p. 2). The primary retention estimate is −0.006 (SE 0.007) against a pre-adoption mean of 0.126 (p. 12, Table 2, Panel A row 1 col 1 and Panel B row 1 col 1). By my arithmetic, a conventional 95% CI runs from about −0.020 to +0.008. The lower end is roughly 2 fewer exits per 100, or about 16% of baseline turnover. The paper discusses only the point estimate ("even if taken at face value"), never the range of effects the data cannot exclude.
- **The introduction contradicts the results section on the composition result.** The introduction says there is no evidence of "practically meaningful" impacts (p. 2). The results section says the composition effect "can be viewed as nontrivial relative to the pre-treatment mean" (p. 12). The text never gives the ratio. By my arithmetic, 0.011 / 0.048 is about a 23% increase in the share of hires from other Missouri districts (p. 14, Table 3, Panel A row 2 col 1 vs. Panel B row 2 col 1).
- **The abstract glosses the composition result.** It says new hires shift "toward more experienced teachers" (p. 1). What is actually measured is origin: "New to district (from another district)" vs. "New to teaching (in Missouri)" (p. 14, Table 3). The comparison group includes out-of-state entrants; the text says only "most of whom are novices" (p. 2). The paper also reports that direct tests of average teacher experience are not significant (p. 21, citing Supplemental Appendix Figure C.4, which I could not review).
- **The early/late adopter definition conflicts (checkable).** The text defines the split by "whether districts adopted the 4DSW by 2020–2021" (p. 6). The Table 1 note says "Late adopters are defined as adopters in 2020–2021 or later" (p. 8). Reading Figure 1 approximately (p. 7), about 19% of districts used the 4DSW in 2020–21 and about 11% in 2019–20. Of 559 districts, that is about 105 vs. about 60, so N = 106 early adopters (p. 8, Table 1) fits the text's inclusive reading. That suggests the note is the error.
- **The Table 6 note describes the wrong model (checkable).** It says "Teacher-level regressions" (p. 20, Table 6 note), but the table reports "Observations (district-years) 2,673". The recruitment models are FTE-weighted district-level regressions (p. 10, Eq. 5; p. 14, Table 3 note). The note looks copied from Table 5.
- **Notation and timing drift in the Methods (checkable).**
  - Eq. 1 uses 4DSW_{jt+1}, and the first stage of Eq. 2 restricts to 4DSW_{jt+1} = 0 (p. 9). But Eq. 4, the preferred specification, is written with 4DSW_{jt} (p. 10), and the text says Eq. 2 "excludes the treatment variable (4DSW_jt)" (p. 9).
  - The text says θ_j and δ_t are fixed effects "as in Equation 1," but Eq. 1 uses Φ_j and ζ_t (p. 6).
  - Consequence: a reader cannot tell from the equations alone whether the retention treatment is dated to year t or t+1.
- **The comparison group is described in two ways (checkable).** Pages 6 and 19 describe the main models as using only not-yet-treated districts as controls. Page 21 says the pre-trend results "reinforce our decision to exclude nonrural, never-treated districts from our main models." That phrasing implies rural never-treated districts are in the main models, which contradicts pp. 6 and 19.
- **Figure axis labels and notes are not self-contained.**
  - Figures 2 and 4 plot exit outcomes ("Any Turnover," "Moved to Different District," "Left Missouri Educator Workforce") under a y-axis labeled "Change in Teacher Retention," and the captions also say "retention" (pp. 13, 17). A negative value means fewer exits, i.e., more retention, which is the opposite of what the axis label suggests.
  - The event-study notes (pp. 13, 15) do not state the CI level, the reference period(s), or any endpoint binning. Event times −6 and −1 are both pinned at zero with no band (Figs. 2–3, pp. 13, 15), and this is not explained.
- **"Strong evidence of parallel pre-trends" is too strong (interpretive).** The text claims this "with small confidence intervals" (p. 11). Failing to reject is not strong evidence. In two-stage/imputation estimators, pre-period coefficients are computed from residuals of a first stage fit on those same untreated observations, so narrow pre-period bands (visibly narrower than post-period bands in Figs. 2–3) are not fully independent evidence. The paper does not discuss this.
- **The saturation prose contradicts itself and rests on point estimates.**
  - One sentence calls the interaction coefficients "consistently small," and the next concedes they "may initially seem large" (p. 19).
  - Scaled by the SD of ≈0.095 (p. 20, Tables 5–6 notes), some point estimates are not small relative to the main effects. For example, SPED moves: −0.099 × 0.095 ≈ −0.009 per SD, against a main effect of 0.013 (p. 20, Table 5, Panel B col 4).
  - For all-subjects turnover, the 95% CI for a one-SD shift is roughly −0.008 to +0.010 (my arithmetic from 0.010 (0.050), Table 5 Panel A col 1). That range is about as large as the main effect of −0.007. "The scope for saturation … is very small" (p. 19) is a point-estimate claim, not a precision claim.
- **The perception-vs-reality conclusion is stronger than the design supports (interpretive).**
  - The intro calls the "disconnect" a "significant information problem" (p. 2), and the conclusion says the findings "highlight a substantial gap between perception and reality" (p. 22).
  - Interviewees' main evidence was "increases in applicants" (p. 2; quote on p. 5). The paper says application data are unavailable (p. 24, fn. 10), so that perception is never tested.
  - The one robust significant result, more hires from other Missouri districts (p. 14, Table 3), is arguably *consistent with* the recruitment advantage superintendents describe. The text does not engage with this.
  - The qualitative section never gives counts behind "overwhelmingly," "predominant view," or "a handful of dissenters" (pp. 4–5), and does not explain how the 22 districts were selected.
- **Many load-bearing robustness claims are asserted in prose and point to the unavailable Supplemental Appendix.** These include covariates (A.2), alternative estimators (A.3–A.5), alternative control groups and salary/experience trends (C, C.4–C.6), the interview-district-only test (D), and the pre-COVID test (E) (pp. 10–11, 20–22). The appendix was not available for this review. Readers of the article alone cannot verify any of these.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- **Must read:** Results pp. 11–14; Table 2 (p. 12), especially Panel A row 1 col 1 with the Panel B baseline; Table 3 (p. 14), especially rows 2–3 in cols 1 and 4. The composition shift and the SPED results are the paper's only non-null findings.
- **Read Figure 5 (p. 18) alongside Table 3 before quoting the composition result.** Visually, the "Moves to District FTEs" estimate drifts toward zero as d grows. From roughly 50 km onward the lower band sits at or below zero, i.e., the result is no longer distinguishable from zero once more spillover-exposed controls are excluded. The text reports only that the bands still include the d = 0 estimate (p. 16). Both statements are true, and together they mean the spillover test is uninformative rather than reassuring.
- **When quoting the retention null, quote the interval, not "no effect."** By my arithmetic, the data do not exclude a reduction of about 2 exits per 100 teacher FTEs (p. 12, Table 2).
- **Do not repeat the abstract's "more experienced teachers" without qualification.** The measured shift is from "new to teaching in Missouri" toward "from another Missouri district" hires (p. 14, Table 3).
- **Flip the sign mentally in Figures 2 and 4.** The y-axis says "retention," but the plotted outcome is exits. Negative values mean fewer exits.
- **Treat the Table 1 early/late split as "adopted by 2020–21 = early"** (p. 6 text), not as the Table 1 note (p. 8) states. Also note that the significant Panel B differences are exactly the outcome variables: any turnover −3.3*, moved −2.6*, new to district −2.2* (p. 8, Table 1 Panel B). The text summarizes Panel B as "much smaller, and most are not statistically significant" (p. 6) without mentioning this.
- **Table 4 (p. 16) reports no baseline out-of-field rate.** Its estimates (−0.021 to −0.031, SEs 0.023–0.025) cannot be judged for magnitude. "No indication that the 4DSW reduces out-of-field teaching" (p. 14) means "imprecise," not "zero."
- **Skimmable:** Background (pp. 3–4) if you know the 4DSW literature; the forbidden-comparisons exposition (pp. 9–10) if you know modern DiD; the interview quotations (pp. 4–5). The quotations convey tone, but the section gives no prevalence counts.
- **Take on trust only knowingly:** every "substantively similar" robustness claim that cites the Supplemental Appendix (pp. 10–11, 20–22). The appendix was not available for this review.

**Detailed Commentary:**

**Organization and navigability.** The paper is short and well signposted. The qualitative section before the quantitative analysis sets up the "perception vs. reality" frame, and the conclusion returns to it. The Results section anchors each claim to a specific panel/row/column, which makes it easy to use. The load-bearing material is concentrated in Tables 2–3 and Figures 2–3 (pp. 12–15). Tables 4–6 and Figures 4–5 serve as checks. A structural drawback is the "Other Considerations" section (pp. 19–22). It contains several substantive validity arguments (control-group choice, salary trends, the interview-district subsample, the pre-COVID sample), but each rests entirely on supplemental exhibits, so it reads as a list of assurances rather than evidence the reader can inspect.

**Fidelity of argument.** Mechanically, the prose reports the tables faithfully: I found no misquoted coefficient. The fidelity problems are about framing.

- *Precision.* The paper repeatedly characterizes the retention null through its point estimate ("very small," "0.6 fewer … per 100," p. 11) and never states what its standard errors allow. The same point-estimate reasoning appears when the text calls vacancy confounding "largely ruled out" by the "very small and statistically insignificant retention estimates" (p. 12). A CI reaching about 2 exits per 100 is not small relative to the 1-per-100 composition shift the paper then interprets.
- *Disconnect framing.* The central interpretive claim is that educators' positive perceptions are contradicted by the data (p. 2, "most interesting takeaway"; p. 22, "substantial gap between perception and reality"). This deserves more hedging than it gets. The perceptions interviewees cite most concretely (applicant volume) are unmeasured (fn. 10). Their retention perceptions concern their own districts, which the paper tests only in an unavailable appendix. And the paper's own significant finding, that adopters draw more experienced in-state movers, supports a recruitment story. The text itself says this effect "can be viewed as nontrivial" (p. 12), yet the introduction's "no evidence of practically meaningful 4DSW impacts" (p. 2) overrides it. The introduction's description of the SPED result as a "boost in special education recruitment" (p. 2) is also firmer than the results section's "marginally significant" (p. 12). That label is accurate for the total SPED new-hire effect (0.022+, p. 14, Table 3 Panel A row 1 col 4); the "from another district" SPED effect is 0.029** (row 2 col 4).

**Abstract fidelity.** The abstract accurately states the question, setting, method, the retention null, and the absence of a workforce-size change. It omits:

- the marginal SPED recruitment result;
- the out-of-field null;
- the spillover tests;
- any sense of precision.

"Shifts toward more experienced teachers" rephrases an origin-based measure. "We show that our findings are unlikely to be driven by saturation effects" is fair as a point-estimate statement. Also, "no evidence … that districts expand their workforce" is inferred from the new-hire *share* (dependent variable defined on p. 14, Table 3 note), not from a model of FTE levels, which the paper does not report in the main text.

**Internal consistency and exhibits.** The tables are internally clean: component rows sum to totals within rounding almost everywhere, and Table 1 difference columns match the group means. The inconsistencies sit in the connective tissue:

- the early/late definition (text vs. Table 1 note);
- the Table 6 note;
- the treatment timing index and fixed-effect symbols across Eqs. 1–4;
- the "exclude nonrural, never-treated" phrasing on p. 21;
- the Table 1 district total of 554 vs. the 559 reported on p. 6.

Figures are honestly scaled; Figures 2–4 use symmetric ±0.10 axes. Note that Figure 5 uses a tighter ±0.025 axis (p. 18), so its bands look visually wider than Figure 4's. The event-study notes are too thin to be self-contained. The Figure 4 any-turnover band widens sharply at roughly 42–52 km (visual reading, p. 17), and the text does not comment on it.

**Density.** The article is lean. A time-constrained reader can get the full empirical content from pp. 11–14 plus Tables 2–3 and Figure 5. The background and methods exposition can be skimmed by specialists.

#### Text–table consistency checks performed

1. "0.6 fewer teacher exits per 100" (p. 11; also p. 2) vs. −0.006 (p. 12, Table 2 Panel A row 1 col 1): **matches**.
2. "1.3 fewer STEM teacher exits per 100" (p. 11) vs. −0.013 (p. 12, Table 2 Panel A row 1 col 3): **matches**.
3. "None of the coefficients in these columns is statistically significant" (p. 11) vs. Table 2 cols 2–4 (p. 12), which have no significance markers: **matches**.
4. Table 2 exits-by-type sum to any turnover, Panel B (p. 12): 0.073+0.053=0.126; 0.067+0.048=0.115; 0.065+0.044=0.109; 0.064+0.046=0.110: **matches**. Panel A estimates also sum within rounding (e.g., −0.005 + −0.001 = −0.006, col 1): **matches**.
5. "Shift is on the order of 1 teacher FTE per 100", offsetting (p. 12) vs. 0.011** and −0.010* (p. 14, Table 3 Panel A rows 2–3 col 1): **matches**.
6. "Marginally significant positive coefficient for special education" (p. 12) vs. 0.022+ (p. 14, Table 3 Panel A row 1 col 4): **matches**.
7. SPED experienced-hire increase "more pronounced… not fully offset" (p. 14 text) vs. 0.029** and −0.007 (p. 14, Table 3 Panel A rows 2–3 col 4): **matches**.
8. Table 3 origin rows sum to all new hires, Panel B (p. 14): col 1 0.048+0.079=0.127 (matches); col 2 0.048+0.074=0.122 vs. 0.121 (rounding); col 4 0.045+0.075=0.120 vs. 0.119 (rounding); **col 3 0.048+0.067=0.115 vs. 0.117 (small mismatch beyond rounding; unexplained)**.
9. Early/late cutoff: text "adopted the 4DSW by 2020–2021" (p. 6) vs. Table 1 note "Late adopters are defined as adopters in 2020–2021 or later" (p. 8): **mismatch**. Figure 1's approximate 2020–21 district share (p. 7) is consistent with N = 106 early adopters under the text's definition.
10. "Large increase in adoption following the 2020–2021 school year, as shown in Figure 1" (p. 6) vs. Figure 1 (p. 7): **ambiguous**. The largest single-year jump visible in the district line is *into* 2020–21 (about 11% to about 19%); later increases are smaller year to year.
11. District counts: "178 of Missouri's 559 districts" (p. 6) and "178 districts (32%)" (p. 2; Fig. 1 label, p. 7) vs. Table 1 N = 376 + 178 = 554 (p. 8): **mismatch of 5 districts, unexplained**. 178/559 = 31.8%, consistent with "32%" and the abstract's "3 in 10": **matches**.
12. Table 1 "Using 2023–2024 Data" (p. 8) with Ever-4DSW N = 178, which is the count "by 2024–2025" (p. 6): **potential mismatch in reference year**. Figure 1 shows about 30.5% in 2023–24 vs. 32% in 2024–25 (visual reading, p. 7).
13. Table 1 difference columns vs. group means (p. 8), all rows in both panels: **match within rounding** (e.g., −5,593 = 2,202 − 7,795; \$3,533 ≈ \$46,553 − \$43,019).
14. "Differences in panel B are much smaller, and most are not statistically significant" (p. 6) vs. Table 1 Panel B (p. 8): **partly matches**. Most differences are unstarred, but several Panel B differences are as large as or larger than their Panel A counterparts (FRPL 6.3 vs. 5.9; Hispanic 5.9 vs. −1.8; suburban 20.4 vs. −25.4 in absolute value). The three starred Panel B differences are all outcome variables.
15. Figure 2 described as showing "small confidence intervals and point estimates near zero" in pre-periods (p. 11) vs. Figure 2 (p. 13): **matches visually**. The y-axis label "Change in Teacher Retention" vs. the plotted exit outcomes is a **labeling inconsistency**.
16. Figure 4 at d = 0 "replicate[s] our main findings in Table 2, column (1)" (p. 17 note) vs. Figure 4 (p. 17): **matches visually** (any turnover ≈ −0.006; exit types near −0.005 and 0).
17. Figure 5 at d = 0 replicates Table 3 col 1 (p. 18 note) vs. Figure 5 (p. 18): **matches visually** (total ≈ 0; moves ≈ +0.011; new to teaching ≈ −0.010). Text says bands "include the original estimates at virtually all values of d" (p. 16): **matches visually**.
18. "151 different estimates… d ∈ [0,150]" and "0–93 miles" (p. 16) vs. Figure 4/5 notes and axes (pp. 17–18): **matches** (150 km ≈ 93 mi). P50 tick near 41 km vs. fn. 13 "half occur within 41 km" (p. 24): **matches visually**.
19. Saturation ρ1 "very similar to what we report in Tables 2 and 3" (p. 19) vs. Table 5 Panel A/B/C 4DSW rows and Table 6 4DSW rows (p. 20) vs. Tables 2–3: **matches** (e.g., −0.007 vs. −0.006; 0.009** vs. 0.011**). Largest relative gap is Table 5 Panel B SPED 0.013 vs. Table 2 row 2 col 4 0.006; both are insignificant.
20. Saturation SD "just 0.10" (p. 19) vs. "roughly 0.095" (p. 20, Tables 5–6 notes): **matches (rounded)**.
21. Interaction coefficients "consistently small and far from statistical significance" (p. 19) vs. Tables 5–6 (p. 20): **significance claim matches** (no interaction is starred). "Small" conflicts with the next sentence ("may initially seem large") and, after SD scaling, is a point-estimate-only claim.
22. Table 6 note "Teacher-level regressions" (p. 20) vs. "Observations (district-years) 2,673" and the district-level recruitment design (p. 10; p. 14 Table 3 note): **mismatch**.
23. Eq. 4 treatment indexed 4DSW_{jt} (p. 10) vs. Eq. 1 4DSW_{jt+1} and first-stage condition 4DSW_{jt+1} = 0 (pp. 6, 9); text "excludes the treatment variable (4DSW_jt)" (p. 9): **notation mismatch**.
24. "θ_j and δ_t are district and year fixed effects, as in Equation 1" (p. 9) vs. Eq. 1's Φ_j and ζ_t (p. 6): **notation mismatch**.
25. Control group: main models use not-yet-treated only (pp. 6, 19) vs. "our decision to exclude nonrural, never-treated districts from our main models" (p. 21): **wording mismatch**.
26. Table 4 observation counts 2,658 / 2,657 / 2,651 (p. 16) vs. 2,673 in Tables 3 and 6 (pp. 14, 20): **unexplained difference**. Table 4 reports no pre-adoption mean, unlike Tables 2–3: **exhibit gap**.
27. Interview sample "36 … 20 superintendents, 4 principals, and 12 teachers in 22 total districts" (p. 4): 20 + 4 + 12 = 36, **matches**. Same 22 districts in the Appendix D test (p. 21): **consistent**.
28. Nowak et al. (2023): "one suburban Colorado district" (p. 23, fn. 2) vs. "negative retention effects in … Denver" (p. 22): **descriptive inconsistency** (minor).
29. Thompson (2025) window "2008–2009 through 2018–2019" (p. 3) vs. "Thompson's data panel ends in 2019" (p. 19): **matches**. "From 33 to 178" districts (p. 3) vs. Figure 1 about 6% in 2018–19 (≈33 of 559) and 178 in 2024–25 (p. 7): **matches approximately (visual reading)**.

---

### Contribution Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The paper gives the most current and most thorough quasi-experimental evidence on whether Missouri's four-day school week (4DSW) changed teacher retention and hiring. Its panel covers the post-COVID wave of adoptions, it uses heterogeneity-robust difference-in-differences, and it tests for spatial spillovers and market saturation. It finds a precisely estimated but not tightly bounded null on retention, no change in the overall new-hire share, and a shift in hiring toward teachers who move in from other Missouri districts. It is a rigorous, policy-relevant addition to a literature with mixed findings, but its retention result largely confirms an earlier Missouri study (Thompson, 2025). Its most quotable framing, a "disconnect" between what educators perceive and what the data show, is somewhat stronger than the measured outcomes can support.

**Strengths:**

- **Timely coverage of the policy-relevant period (checkable).** The panel runs from 2008–2009 through 2023–2024 (p. 5, Data), capturing the expansion "from 33 to 178" Missouri 4DSW districts that happened after the earlier Missouri study's panel ends in 2018–2019 (p. 3, Background). By 2024–2025, 178 of 559 districts used the 4DSW (p. 6; Figure 1, p. 7). The earlier study cannot speak to this surge in adoptions, the one that motivates today's policy debate.
- **Adds recruitment and hire composition to a literature that has focused on retention (checkable).** The paper's clearest new empirical result is the origin split of new hires: +0.011 (SE 0.003) in the FTE share of hires from other Missouri districts and −0.010 (SE 0.004) in hires new to teaching in Missouri (p. 14, Table 3, Panel A rows 2–3, col. 1). Against pre-adoption means of 0.048 and 0.079 (p. 14, Table 3, Panel B), these are relative changes of about +23% and −13% (reviewer's arithmetic from Table 3).
- **Credible modern design, well matched to the setting (checkable plus interpretive).** Treated districts are compared only with not-yet-treated districts. That choice is motivated by large level differences between adopters and never-adopters (p. 8, Table 1 Panel A; for example, average salary of \$44,718 vs. \$54,909). It is implemented with Gardner et al.'s two-stage estimator, which blocks "forbidden comparisons" (pp. 9–10, Methods). Retention event studies show flat pre-trends from event time −6 to −1 (p. 13, Figure 2). For readers, this makes the retention null hard to attribute to specification choices.
- **Takes spillovers and saturation seriously, which matters for this policy.** The motivating story in the interviews is competitive ("keeping up with the Joneses," p. 4). The Butts-style spillover exclusions over 0–150 km (pp. 16–18, Figures 4–5) and the commuting-zone saturation interactions (p. 20, Tables 5–6) test exactly the mechanisms a skeptic would raise. For the retention result, the spillover-adjusted estimates stay near zero across distances (p. 17, Figure 4).
- **The mixed-methods framing is distinctive and useful.** The 36 interviews (20 superintendents, 4 principals, 12 teachers in 22 districts, conducted October 2021–April 2023; p. 4) document what adopters believe the policy does. The paper then tests that belief against administrative data rather than assuming it, a model for evaluating policies justified by practitioner perception.
- **Honest positioning relative to the closest prior work (checkable).** The authors state plainly that Thompson (2025) already found null retention effects in Missouri and Oklahoma. They present their work as complementing and extending it (p. 3) and note where their saturation and pre-COVID results mirror his (p. 19; p. 22).

**Weaknesses:**

- **The retention null is informative but less tight than the text implies (checkable plus interpretive).** The main estimate is −0.006 (SE 0.007) against a pre-adoption turnover mean of 0.126 (p. 12, Table 2, col. 1, Panels A and B, row 1). A conventional 95% interval (reviewer's calculation) runs from about −0.020 to +0.008. That does not rule out a reduction in turnover of up to roughly 16% of baseline. For STEM teachers, −0.013 (SE 0.008) against a mean of 0.109 (p. 12, Table 2, col. 3) does not rule out reductions of roughly a quarter. "No evidence that the 4DSW improves teacher retention" (Abstract, p. 1) is accurate. "No evidence of practically meaningful 4DSW impacts" (p. 2) is a stronger claim than these intervals support, because the interval still includes effects many policymakers would consider meaningful.
- **Incremental relative to Thompson (2025) on the core retention question (interpretive).** Of the paper's results, the retention null, the absence of saturation moderation (p. 19), and the pre-COVID null (p. 22, Supplemental Appendix E, not available for this review) replicate or extend findings already published for Missouri. Replication has real value, but the paper's novelty rests mainly on the newer years, the recruitment outcomes, and the qualitative component.
- **"Recruitment" is measured narrowly.** The recruitment outcome is the new-hire share of FTEs (p. 10, Eq. 5). That measure is driven by vacancies and district demand, not by labor supply. The authors acknowledge that applicant data are unavailable (p. 23–24, note 10) and that recruitment estimates are "imperfect ex ante" (p. 10). As a result, the paper cannot test the claim interviewees most often made, that the 4DSW produced more applicants (for example, "more applications for our positions than we've ever had," p. 5). It also does not measure the quality of new hires.
- **The "perception vs. reality" contrast partly compares different constructs (interpretive).** Interviewees cite applicant pools, teacher satisfaction, and anecdotes about experienced teachers returning (p. 5). The quantitative outcomes are exits and hire shares. The paper's one robust positive finding, more hires from other Missouri districts (p. 14, Table 3), is arguably *consistent with* what superintendents report about attracting experienced teachers. The paper calls the disconnect "perhaps the most interesting takeaway" and says it "indicates a significant information problem" (p. 2). That overstates how cleanly the two data sources contradict each other.
- **The composition result is fragile under the spillover adjustment (checkable from the figure; interpretive about meaning).** In Figure 5 (p. 18, "Moves to District FTEs" panel), the confidence band for the from-another-district estimate includes zero from roughly 50 km onward. Its point estimate drifts toward zero at larger distances. Half of observed cross-district moves fall within 41 km (p. 23, note 13). The authors correctly note that the bands include the original estimates (p. 16), but the bands also include zero. Readers cannot tell from the paper whether the shift reflects an absolute draw of movers into 4DSW districts or partly a relative effect that operates by pulling teachers away from nearby comparison districts.
- **"More experienced" is inferred from where hires came from, not measured directly.** The abstract states that "the composition of new hires shifts toward more experienced teachers" (p. 1). The table variable is where hires came from, another Missouri district versus new to teaching in Missouri (p. 14, Table 3). The paper describes the latter group as "most of whom are novices" (p. 2) without reporting that share in the main text. The direct check on average teacher experience is described as not significant and "small and underpowered" (p. 21, citing Supplemental Appendix Figures C.4–C.5, which were not available for this review).
- **Special-education results are emphasized despite many tests (checkable).** The SPED coefficients, 0.022 (SE 0.012, p < .10) for all new hires and 0.029 (SE 0.006) for hires from other districts against a mean of 0.045 (p. 14, Table 3, col. 4), are called "the most favorable" results (p. 14) and are mentioned in the Introduction (p. 2). This comes from a 12-cell table, after the authors themselves cite von Hippel & Schuetze's warning about "no, but" subgroup inference for the retention table (p. 11).

**Guidance for Readers:**

**Cite this paper for:**

- The best current evidence that, among Missouri districts that adopted a 4DSW through 2024–2025, adoption did not measurably reduce teacher turnover. The point estimate is −0.006 on a base of 0.126 (p. 12, Table 2), and pre-trends are flat (p. 13, Figure 2).
- Evidence that adopting districts did not expand the teacher workforce, measured by new-hire FTE share: 0.001 (SE 0.006) (p. 14, Table 3, row 1, col. 1).
- Suggestive evidence that 4DSW adopters hire relatively more teachers from other Missouri districts and fewer who are new to Missouri teaching (p. 14, Table 3, rows 2–3). Cite this with the spillover caveat from Figure 5 (p. 18).
- Evidence that retention effects in Missouri do not appear to depend on how common the 4DSW already was locally at adoption. For example, the 4DSW × Prevalence coefficient for any turnover is 0.010 (SE 0.050), and a one-SD change in prevalence is about 0.095 (p. 20, Table 5 and note).
- A documented case in which practitioners report strong staffing benefits from a policy that administrative data do not confirm on the retention margin (pp. 4–5 vs. p. 12).

**Do not lean on it for:**

- "The 4DSW has no meaningful effect on retention." The 95% interval admits reductions of about 2 points on a base of about 12.6 (p. 12, Table 2). The finding is "no detectable effect," not a tight zero.
- "The 4DSW does not help recruitment." Applicant flows and hire quality are not observed (p. 23–24, note 10). Hire share mixes supply with district demand (p. 10).
- "The 4DSW attracts more experienced teachers." The measured shift is by origin, not by experience, and the direct experience outcome is described as insignificant (p. 21).
- "Four-day weeks help special-education staffing." The result is one marginal and one significant cell among many subgroup tests (p. 14, Table 3, col. 4).
- Student-achievement harms or cost-benefit conclusions. The paper cites other studies for these (p. 4; p. 22) and estimates neither.
- The policy recommendation to "facilitate a natural transition away from the 4DSW" (p. 22). This goes beyond what the paper estimates and depends on outcomes it does not measure.
- National generalization. The adopters are small, rural, lower-paying districts (p. 8, Table 1 Panel A). The 178 adopting districts contain only 13% of Missouri teachers and 12% of students (p. 7, Figure 1 labels). Adoption by larger or higher-paying districts elsewhere, or where recruitment effects were found (Texas, p. 22), may differ.

**Open questions that remain unresolved:**

- Is the hire-composition shift zero-sum across the state? Which districts lose the teachers who move into 4DSW districts, and are they rural five-day-week neighbors?
- Does the 4DSW change applicant volume or hire quality, the margins interviewees actually cite (p. 5)? This requires application-level data (p. 23–24, note 10).
- Do effects vary by how the 4DSW is implemented (instructional hours, which day is off, teacher duties on the fifth day)? The paper treats adoption as binary.
- Why do Missouri, Colorado, and Oklahoma show nulls, Oregon and a Colorado district show negative effects, and Texas and Arkansas show positive effects (p. 3; p. 22)? No cross-state explanation is offered.
- Do teachers value the 4DSW as a non-wage amenity that affects their well-being without affecting mobility? The paper raises this possibility (p. 22) but cannot test it.
- Supplemental Appendices A–E (alternative estimators, covariates, control groups, interview-district reanalysis, pre-COVID estimates) were not available for this review. The claims in the main text that rely on them (pp. 10–11, 19–22) could not be checked here.

**Minor checkable inconsistencies a citing reader may notice:**

- The early/late adopter cutoff is described as "adopted the 4DSW by 2020–2021" = early (p. 6). The Table 1 note defines late adopters as "adopters in 2020–2021 or later" (p. 8).
- Table 1 Panel A counts 376 + 178 = 554 districts (p. 8), while the text refers to 559 Missouri districts (p. 6).
- Nowak et al. (2023) is described as studying "one suburban Colorado district" (p. 23, note 2) but as studying "Denver" in the Conclusion (p. 22).
- The Table 6 note says "Teacher-level regressions," but the table reports district-year observations (p. 20).

**Detailed Commentary:**

**Novelty.** The question, whether the 4DSW improves teacher retention, is not new. Neither is the setting of Missouri, which Thompson (2025) studied through 2018–2019 with null retention results (p. 3). What is new falls into three parts. First, the panel runs through 2023–2024 and so covers the period in which adopting districts grew from 33 to 178 (p. 3). Adopters in that later wave stated a primary motive of teacher staffing (p. 1; p. 4), so the extension is substantive, not cosmetic. Second, the paper adds recruitment outcomes, especially where new hires come from, which the retention-focused literature largely lacks. Third, it pairs estimation with interviews so that practitioners' causal beliefs can be compared directly with the estimates. The methods, two-stage DiD, Butts spillover exclusions, and saturation interactions, are applications of existing tools rather than methodological contributions. They are chosen well for a policy whose effects plausibly depend on how neighboring districts respond.

**Significance.** The stakes are real. Missouri has an active legislative debate (SB727 requires voter approval for 4DSW use in communities of at least 30,000 residents and adds 1% to 2% of prior state aid for five-day districts; p. 3). Other studies find that the 4DSW harms achievement (p. 4). If the policy's main justification, staffing, does not show up in retention, adopting districts face a worse trade-off than they believe. Read at the credible strength of its estimates, this paper tells the field that Missouri adopters did not see detectable retention gains or workforce expansion, and saw at most a modest reshuffling of hires toward in-state movers. That should shift priors toward skepticism about the 4DSW as a staffing tool in rural Midwestern settings. It does not establish that the policy is useless for staffing. The retention interval still allows reductions of about 16% of baseline turnover (reviewer's calculation from p. 12, Table 2), and the supply-side outcomes practitioners care about most are not observed.

**The gap between the quotable claim and the best-supported claim.** The most quotable line is that the "disconnect" between interviews and data "indicates a significant information problem and suggests better information could lead to better policy decisions" (p. 2). The best-supported claim is narrower: across adopters, teacher exit rates and new-hire shares did not change detectably. The step from one to the other requires that interviewees' beliefs concern the outcomes the paper measures. Many do not. The quotes emphasize applicant volume, satisfaction, and bringing back teachers who left for higher pay (p. 5). The paper's one significant hiring result, more hires from other Missouri districts (p. 14, Table 3), is a plausible statistical counterpart to those anecdotes. The authors' own reconciliation, that teachers may value the 4DSW but not enough to change where they work (p. 22), is sensible and weakens the "information problem" reading. Readers should cite the paper for the absence of detectable retention effects, not as proof that practitioners are misinformed about the policy's effects on their own districts. The interview-district reanalysis (Supplemental Appendix D, not available here) is described as finding similar nulls (p. 21), and this partly addresses whether interviewed districts are unusual. Even so, it cannot address the mismatch between what interviewees talked about and what the data measure.

**Robustness of the new finding.** The composition shift is the paper's main new empirical result, so readers should know how firm it is. In the main specification it is well estimated (p. 14, Table 3, rows 2–3, col. 1) and appears in the event study (p. 15, Figure 3), where post-adoption point estimates for hires from another district sit slightly above zero and the bands widen at longer horizons. Under spillover-robust estimation, however, the band includes zero beyond about 50 km, near or above the median move distance of 41 km (p. 18, Figure 5; p. 23, note 13). One natural reading is economic rather than statistical. If 4DSW districts draw teachers from nearby five-day districts, those neighbors are "treated" through spillovers, and a naive comparison with them overstates the absolute effect. The paper's conclusion of "no evidence of meaningful bias" (p. 16) is defensible as a test of equality with the original estimate. It does not show that the composition effect survives. Whether this reshuffling helps students or the state is unaddressed, because the paper does not trace where the movers came from or measure their effectiveness.

**Generalizability.** The comparison is entirely among districts that adopt at some point, using not-yet-treated districts as controls (p. 6). The resulting estimate is the effect of adoption timing within a population of small, rural, lower-paying districts. Those districts have higher baseline turnover (16.9% vs. 14.2%) and much lower average salaries than never-adopters (p. 8, Table 1 Panel A). This is the right population for Missouri's current debate. The finding transfers more doubtfully to states where adopters differ, and the paper itself notes Texas as the one state with "meaningful positive effects" (p. 22). The authors are mostly honest about these boundaries. They do not claim the interviews are representative (p. 5), and they frame the study as one state's evidence within a mixed literature (p. 3; p. 22). The abstract's "3 in 10 districts" (p. 1) could leave a reader with an inflated sense of scale. By teachers the share is 13% (p. 7, Figure 1), which matters for any statewide labor-market interpretation.

**Standing in the literature.** For Missouri, this paper is now the most complete causal evidence on 4DSW staffing effects. It covers more years, more adopters, and more outcomes than Thompson (2025), with consistent results where the two overlap (p. 22). Nationally, it is one strong data point in a literature the authors summarize as mixed: small positive effects in Arkansas, larger positive effects in Texas, nulls in Colorado and in Missouri/Oklahoma, and negative effects in Oregon and one Colorado district (p. 3; p. 22). It moves the weight of evidence toward "little or no retention effect" but does not settle the national question. The most valuable follow-on work it sets up is supply-side: applicant data, hire quality, and a statewide accounting of where cross-district movers come from. That work would determine whether the 4DSW is an ineffective staffing tool or a reallocative one that helps adopters at their neighbors' expense. Cross-state work explaining the Texas–Missouri contrast would also be valuable.

**Overall.** This is a careful, well-identified, policy-relevant paper that deserves citation as the reference for Missouri's post-COVID experience with the 4DSW on retention and hiring. Its contribution is solid but incremental on the headline retention question. Its most distinctive framing, perception versus reality, is somewhat stronger than its measures support. Its genuinely new empirical result, the hire-composition shift, is less robust than the abstract suggests. Hence Adequate, at the upper end of that category.

---

### Reproducibility Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The paper documents its estimator clearly: a Gardner et al. (2024) two-stage difference-in-differences with not-yet-treated controls, district and year fixed effects, district-clustered errors, and FTE weights for the district-level models. Its point estimates are internally consistent with the prose. But the main text contains none of the verification infrastructure that current journals expect: no data availability statement, no access pathway for the restricted Missouri DESE records, no replication package or code link, and no software statement. Several steps in building the outcomes, the sample, and the event studies are left unstated, so a replicator with data access would have to guess at them. The headline retention null is probably robust to those guesses. The statistically significant finding on the composition of new hires depends more on undocumented definitions and on how the standard errors were computed.

**Strengths:**

- **Data sources are named (checkable).** Teacher records are individual-level administrative panel data from the Missouri Department of Elementary and Secondary Education (DESE), covering 2008–09 through 2023–24. District covariates come from the NCES Common Core of Data, and 4DSW adoption dates come from DESE (p. 5, Data section; pp. 5–6). Commuting zones use the Fowler (2024) delineation (p. 19; reference list).
- **The treatment coding is described and cross-checked (checkable).** The DESE adoption list was checked against an independent list kept by Dr. Jon Turner, and "a handful of discrepancies" were resolved. The two districts that reverted to a five-day week are named as a special case, and results are reported as insensitive to dropping them (footnote 6, p. 23).
- **The estimator is written out step by step (checkable).** Equations 2–4 give the first stage on untreated observations, the residualization, and the second stage (pp. 9–10). Equation 5 gives the district-level recruitment analog with FTE weights and its rationale (p. 10). The paper explicitly says it uses no covariates in the main models (p. 9), states the not-yet-treated comparison group (p. 6), and clusters standard errors at the district level "in all models" (p. 9).
- **The main exhibits report uncertainty and sample sizes (checkable).** Tables 2–6 report point estimates with standard errors, significance thresholds, and observation counts. Tables 2 and 3 report pre-adoption means, which lets readers scale effect sizes. Examples: 138,633 teacher-years in Table 2, column 1 (p. 12), and 2,673 district-years in Table 3 (p. 14).
- **Prose and tables agree (checkable).** "0.6 fewer teacher exits per 100" (p. 11) matches −0.006 (0.007) in Table 2, row 1, column 1 (p. 12). "1.3 fewer STEM teacher exits" (p. 11) matches −0.013 (0.008) in Table 2, column 3. The roughly 1-per-100 composition shift (p. 12) matches 0.011** (0.003) and −0.010* (0.004) in Table 3, rows 2–3, column 1 (p. 14).
- **Robustness is spread across several estimators and control groups (checkable as claims, not as results).** The paper points to the Borusyak et al., Wooldridge, and Callaway–Sant'Anna estimators (Supplemental Tables A.3–A.5), added covariates (A.2), district aggregation (A.1), alternative control groups (Appendix C), the interview-district subsample (Appendix D), and a pre-COVID window (Appendix E) (pp. 11, 19–22). The spillover sensitivity is shown in full over 151 distance values from 0 to 150 km (Figures 4–5, pp. 16–18). That is a transparent way to show a sensitivity analysis.

**Weaknesses:**

- **No data availability statement and no access pathway (checkable absence).** I read the end-matter on pp. 23–24: Acknowledgments, ORCID iDs, Funding (IES Grant R305C240007), Declaration of Conflicting Interests, and a one-line Supplemental Material notice. None of it says whether or how another researcher could get the DESE teacher records, whether a data-use agreement governs them, or whom to contact. The Acknowledgments thank the PRiME Center at Saint Louis University "for their collaboration" (p. 23) but do not describe any data role.
- **No code, replication package, or software environment (checkable absence).** Nowhere in the main text or end-matter is there a repository link, a statement that code is available (even on request), or the software and package used for the two-stage estimator or the alternative estimators. The only "available upon request" language covers a single robustness check, the exclusion of Independence School District (footnote 7, p. 23).
- **The treatment-year file is not published (checkable absence; interpretive significance).** Adoption years for the 178 districts are not tabulated in the main text. Only aggregate counts appear, in Figure 1 (p. 7). This list is not confidential, it is the single most important constructed variable, and the paper hand-reconciled it against a second source (footnote 6, p. 23). Without it, even a replicator who obtains DESE data cannot reproduce the treatment coding.
- **The analytic sample is not fully pinned down (checkable ambiguities).**
  - Missouri has 559 districts (p. 6), but Table 1's panels sum to 376 + 178 = 554 (p. 8). The five-district gap is not explained.
  - The main sample appears to be ever-adopters only, with not-yet-treated districts as controls (p. 6). Yet p. 21 describes the decision as excluding "nonrural, never-treated districts," which blurs whether any rural never-treated districts are in the main models.
  - Early and late adopters are defined inconsistently. The text defines early adopters as adopting "by 2020–2021" (p. 6), while the Table 1 note defines late adopters as "adopters in 2020–2021 or later" (p. 8).
  - The two reverting districts are coded "always treated" (footnote 6, p. 23). That term is ambiguous in a staggered DiD: it could mean treated from their adoption year onward, or excluded from the first stage altogether.
- **Outcome definitions leave edge cases open (interpretive, based on checkable text).**
  - An exit means not being "present in the district in year t+1" (p. 6). The paper does not say how it treats teachers who stay in the district but fall below the 0.75 FTE threshold, or who move into non-teaching roles.
  - "New to teaching (in Missouri)" is not defined for returners who left the Missouri system and later came back. The paper also does not say how new hires are classified in the first panel year, 2008–09.
  - "High-need" includes "STEM-adjacent fields (e.g., career and technical education and applied-science fields)" (p. 11), but no course or certification codes are given. The column 3 (STEM) and column 4 (SPED) samples sum to 67,899 teacher-years, more than the 67,391 in column 2 (Table 2, p. 12; my arithmetic). So teachers must appear in more than one field, and the rule for assigning them is not stated.
  - The out-of-field indicator depends on matching certifications to assignments (footnote 12, p. 24), and the crosswalk is not described.
- **Timing notation is inconsistent across the equations (checkable).** Equation 1 uses 4DSW_{jt+1} for the retention outcome (p. 6), and the first-stage restriction on p. 9 conditions on 4DSW_{jt+1} = 0. The text immediately after Equation 2 says the model "excludes the treatment variable (4DSW_jt)," and Equation 4 is written with 4DSW_jt (pp. 9–10). There is a related tension. Table 1 reports 2023–24 turnover rates (p. 8), but the administrative panel ends in 2023–24 (p. 5) and exits are defined forward-looking, relative to t+1 (p. 6). A replicator has to infer which timing convention applies to each exhibit.
- **The event-study specification is not stated (checkable absence).** Figures 2 and 3 plot event times from −6 to +6 (pp. 13, 15). Neither the text nor the figure notes gives the event window, how endpoints are binned, the reference period(s), or the confidence-interval level. On inspection, the confidence bands collapse to zero at both event time −1 and event time −6 (Figure 2, p. 13; Figure 3, p. 15). That suggests two normalizations or a binned endpoint, but the paper does not say which.
- **Standard-error details are incomplete (checkable absence).** The paper says only that errors are clustered by district (p. 9). It does not say whether the second-stage errors correct for the estimated first-stage fixed effects, which the two-stage method requires for valid inference. It also does not report the number of clusters or of treated districts per regression.
- **Spillover and saturation measures are under-specified (checkable absence).** The spillover indicator uses a distance d in kilometers (p. 16), but the geographic reference points (district centroids, office locations, or something else) are not stated. Nor is how the "mover distance distribution" behind the percentile axis in Figures 4–5 was computed (p. 17, figure note; footnote 13, p. 24). The paper does not say how districts that cross county or CZ lines are assigned to commuting zones (p. 19). The Table 6 note says "Teacher-level regressions" while reporting 2,673 district-years (p. 20), which looks like a copy error from Table 5.
- **Several claims rest on material a reader cannot check.** These include localization of the teacher labor market in Missouri ("results suppressed for brevity," p. 16), robustness to including staff below 0.75 FTE (footnote 5, p. 23), and the exclusion of Independence SD (footnote 7, p. 23). All robustness results in Appendices A–E are described only qualitatively in the main text. I did not have access to the supplement, so I cannot judge how fully it documents them.
- **The qualitative component has no protocol or codebook in the main text (checkable absence).** The paper reports 36 interviewees (20 superintendents, 4 principals, 12 teachers) in 22 districts, interviewed between October 2021 and April 2023, with deductive coding (p. 4). It gives no interview protocol, recruitment frame or response rate, codebook, or ethics-review statement.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- **Treat the retention null as the most verifiable claim.** It is a tightly bounded null: −0.006 (0.007) against a pre-adoption mean of 0.126 (Table 2, p. 12), with flat event-study pre- and post-periods (Figure 2, p. 13). Reasonable choices about the exit definition or sample would be unlikely to produce a large effect. Still, no exact number here can be independently reproduced without DESE access and the authors' code.
- **Treat the composition-shift result with more reserve.** The findings are 0.011** and −0.010* in Table 3, rows 2–3 (p. 14), and they rest on three things the paper does not fully specify: how "new to district" and "new to teaching in Missouri" are defined (including returners), how the standard errors account for the first stage, and the FTE weighting. Before relying on these results, ask the authors for the exact new-hire classification rules and the software and command used for estimation and inference. Also check whether the result survives in the supplemental alternative estimators, which I could not inspect.
- **Treat the special-education recruitment result as fragile.** It is 0.022+ (0.012) in Table 3, row 1, column 4, and 0.029** (0.006) in row 2 (p. 14). It depends on a field classification with no published codes. In the saturation model, the corresponding main 4DSW coefficient for all new SPED hires is 0.015 (0.014), not significant (Table 6, Panel A, column 4, p. 20).
- **Request the adoption-year list.** It is non-confidential and should be requestable, and it is enough to reproduce Figure 1 (p. 7) and the Table 1 group definitions (p. 8), and to check the 376/178/559 district accounting (pp. 6, 8).
- **Replicators with DESE access should resolve these ambiguities with the authors first:**
  - the treatment timing convention for retention versus recruitment (pp. 6, 9–10);
  - the event-study window, binning, and reference periods (Figures 2–3);
  - the handling of the two reverting districts (footnote 6);
  - whether any rural never-treated districts are in the main control group (p. 21);
  - how Table 3, columns 2–4, handle districts with zero field-specific FTE, given that Table 4's N varies from 2,651 to 2,658 while Table 3's does not (pp. 14, 16).
- **Regard the spillover (Figures 4–5) and saturation (Tables 5–6) analyses as not reproducible from the text alone.** The distance metric and the CZ assignment rule are unspecified. Their qualitative conclusion (no detectable bias or moderation) is plausible given the narrow confidence bands, but you cannot rebuild the exhibits.
- **Take the qualitative evidence as illustrative rather than auditable.** Its role in the argument is contextual, and the paper says it does not claim the interviewed districts are representative (p. 5).

**Detailed Commentary:**

**Data availability and access.** This is a standard restricted-data education-policy paper. The core teacher panel is individual-level state administrative data that cannot be posted publicly, and the lack of a public dataset is not a failing in itself. What journal-era norms do expect is a data availability statement that names the custodian and the application route. That lets a would-be replicator know whether replication is possible at all. The main text and end-matter (pp. 23–24) contain nothing of the kind. The paper names DESE as the source (p. 5), and the funding note links the work to an IES grant (p. 23). A reader cannot tell from the article whether the DESE data were obtained under a research agreement open to other researchers, through a university–state partnership, or through some other arrangement. The public pieces (the CCD covariates and Fowler's CZ delineation) are named, though I found no CCD dataset citation in the reference list. The one constructed dataset that could have been released at no confidentiality cost is the district-by-year adoption file, reconciled across two sources (footnote 6, p. 23). It was not released, at least not in the main text. That is the clearest missed opportunity, because treatment coding in staggered-adoption designs is where replications most often diverge.

**Code and computation.** The main text and end-matter contain no replication package, no repository link, and no software or package statement. The methods are not computationally exotic: two-stage DiD, three alternative staggered-DiD estimators, and a loop over 151 distance thresholds. The absence of code therefore matters less for reproducing the logic than it would for, say, a Bayesian model. But the exact inference matters here. The paper's two statistically significant main results (Table 3, rows 2–3, column 1, p. 14) depend on standard errors that, under Gardner's two-stage method, must account for the first-stage fixed-effect estimates. The paper says only that errors are clustered by district (p. 9). Whether the corrected variance was used cannot be determined from the text, and that bears directly on the significance stars. One minor point: footnote 5 (p. 23) says a random assignment was drawn for the "very small number" of teachers in multiple districts, with no seed reported. This is immaterial to the results but worth recording.

**Variable and sample construction.** The paper gives the main construction rules: the 0.75 FTE full-time threshold (p. 6), identification of teachers from DESE position codes (p. 6), exits defined as absence from the district in t+1 (p. 6), exits split into within-Missouri moves and exits from the Missouri workforce (p. 6; footnote 11, p. 24), new-hire shares as ratios of new-teacher FTE to total FTE (Table 3 note, p. 14), and out-of-field status as a mismatch between certification and assignment (footnote 12, p. 24). This is enough to build an approximate analytic file. It is not enough to build the same file. The position codes, the course and certification codes defining the STEM, STEM-adjacent, and SPED groups, and the certification–assignment crosswalk are not listed. The multiple-field overlap is implied by the Table 2 Ns but not explained. Edge cases in the exit and new-hire definitions (FTE falling below threshold, moves into non-teaching roles, returners, the first panel year) are not addressed. There are also small checkable inconsistencies a careful replicator will hit. The district counts differ (559 in the text versus 554 across Table 1's panels; pp. 6, 8). The early/late cutoff is stated two different ways (pp. 6, 8). Table 1 reports 2023–24 turnover even though the panel ends in 2023–24 and exits are defined forward-looking (pp. 5–6, 8). None of these threatens the paper's conclusions, but each is a place where a replication would have to guess.

**Specification transparency.** This is the paper's strongest dimension. Equations 1–7 (pp. 6, 9–10, 16, 19) state the estimating equations, the fixed-effect structure, the first-stage estimation sample, the second-stage regressor, the district-level weights, and the spillover and saturation augmentations. The paper also explains why controls are omitted (p. 9). From this description, a competent analyst could re-run the headline two-stage specification. Three gaps remain. First, the treatment timing index changes between Equation 1 and the first-stage restriction (t+1) and Equation 4 (t) (pp. 6, 9–10). Second, the event-study design (window, binning, and reference periods) is unstated, even though Figures 2–3 appear to normalize at two event times (−1 and −6, pp. 13, 15). Third, the spillover distance and the CZ assignment rule are not operationalized. The Table 6 note's "Teacher-level regressions" label (p. 20) conflicts with the table's district-year Ns and should be read as a labeling slip rather than a different model, though that is an inference.

**Results reporting and verifiability.** The main tables report what readers need to judge magnitude and precision: coefficients, standard errors, Ns, and pre-adoption means. The event-study and spillover figures show the full estimate paths rather than selected points. The claims fall into three tiers of verifiability. The main-text point estimates and their internal consistency can be checked from the paper, and they check out. The robustness claims that carry much of the paper's credibility (alternative estimators, control groups, covariates, the interview-district subsample, the pre-COVID window) are described qualitatively and depend on supplemental Appendices A–E. I did not have access to those appendices, so this review cannot say whether they document the robustness results fully. A small set of claims ("results suppressed for brevity," "available upon request," "qualitatively similar" when including staff below 0.75 FTE; pp. 16, 23) cannot be verified from anything published.

**Overall calibration.** Weighing all this, I rate the paper **Adequate**. Specification transparency is good, and the headline null is simple, bounded, and plausibly robust, so the documentation gaps do not prevent readers from understanding or approximately verifying the central retention result. The rating would be higher with a data availability statement, a documented access pathway, a released adoption-year file, and a stated software environment or deposited code. Those are ordinary expectations for a 2026 EEPA article, and their absence keeps the paper from "Strong." Confidence is moderate rather than high mainly because the Supplemental Appendices were unavailable to me. They may resolve some of the construction and event-study ambiguities noted above, or they may not.
